story: In 1910, astronomers Henry Norris Russell, Edward Charles Pickering, and Williamina Fleming analyzed 40 Eridani B, discovering a dim white star with high surface temperature. When plotted on Russell's luminosity diagram, it sat in an impossible lower-left corner. A star with such blistering surface heat should radiate immense light unless its total surface area was tiny, packing an entire star's mass into an Earth-sized volume. Arthur Eddington noted that a matchbox of its core material would weigh a ton. Quantum physics later revealed that electron degeneracy pressure counteracts gravity in these dense stellar remnants. Today, white dwarfs like Sirius B, van Maanen's Star, and Procyon B represent the final evolutionary stage for most stars. Telescopes even reveal white dwarfs like G29-38 and WD 1145+017 actively accreting tidally disrupted rocky planetesimals, shredding remnant solar systems long after their stars have died.
angle: When a star dies, it shrinks into an Earth-sized core so dense that its combination of scorching heat and dim light broke early 20th-century physics.
disputed: Crystallized mass fraction of BPM 37093: 1995/2004 asteroseismological estimates suggested around 90%, but other studies indicate a range between 32% and 82%; attribute as 'estimates range from 32% to 90%'.

Dominant mechanism for Type Ia supernovae: source S1 notes three possible mechanisms (stable accretion, white dwarf collisions, or shell ignition); attribute as 'the exact dominant mechanism remains unconfirmed'.
